Matplotlib has no built-in grouped-stacked bar type, but you can build one: give each subgroup (e.g. X/Y) its own x-offset, and within each offset use `bottom=` to stack the categories on top of each other.

```python
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x = np.arange(len(groups)); width = 0.35
for i, sub in enumerate(subgroups):
    bottom = np.zeros(len(groups))
    for cat in categories:
        vals = df.loc[df.sub == sub, cat].values
        plt.bar(x + i*width, vals, width, bottom=bottom, label=f'{sub}-{cat}')
        bottom += vals
plt.xticks(x + width/2, groups); plt.legend()
```

The outer loop places a bar cluster at `x + i*width` (the "grouped" part); the inner loop stacks segments via `bottom` (the "stacked" part). This reproduces the Excel layout. Alternatives: Plotly Express with `barmode='stack'` plus a facet/offset dimension, or calling `DataFrame.plot(kind='bar', stacked=True)` once per subgroup on the same Axes with manual x-shifts.

For multi-output regression these two are not guaranteed to match, because of how `squared=False` and multi-output averaging interact. `mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred, squared=False)` computes RMSE **per output column, then averages the per-column RMSEs**. Method 2 computes the overall MSE (averaged across outputs) **first, then takes a single sqrt**. Since sqrt is concave, sqrt-then-average differs from average-then-sqrt (Jensen's inequality) — that's your gap. Neither is "wrong"; they answer different questions.

To get one unambiguous number, pick explicitly:

```python
import numpy as np
rmse_per_target = np.sqrt(((y_test - y_pred) ** 2).mean(axis=0))  # then average these
rmse_pooled = np.sqrt(((y_test - y_pred) ** 2).mean())             # single pooled RMSE
```

Report which one you used, since "RMSE of a multi-output model" is ambiguous without specifying whether it's the mean of per-target RMSEs or the RMSE of pooled residuals — that ambiguity, not a bug, is the source of your discrepancy.

ONNX only stores the forward computation graph (a DAG of ops), not autograd metadata, so there is no backward graph to reconstruct from a plain `.onnx` file — this is inherent to the format, not a missing switch.

Your two practical options: (1) Keep the differentiable model in PyTorch (`nn.Module`) and only export to ONNX for inference, i.e. don't round-trip through ONNX for training. (2) Use **onnxruntime-training** (`torch-ort` / `ORTModule`): you wrap an `nn.Module`, and ONNX Runtime exports it internally and builds the corresponding gradient graph automatically during that step. You're correct that this needs the original `nn.Module` source, not an already-exported static `.onnx` file, because gradient-graph construction happens at export time, not by inspecting a finished ONNX file.

If you truly only have a `.onnx` file with no source model, remaining options are numerical differentiation, or converting back to a framework model (e.g. `onnx2torch`) to regain PyTorch autograd, or hand-deriving analytic gradients as you mentioned wanting to avoid.

Nothing in your code inserts a real space — `str.translate` substitutes characters 1-for-1, so `"16".translate(SUB)` yields exactly two glyphs, `₁₆`, with no separator. Confirm with `len(sub_base)` / `repr(sub_base)`: you'll see 2 characters, no whitespace.

The gap you see is a font/rendering artifact: most terminal and console fonts don't kern adjacent Unicode subscript digits tightly, so two of them side by side can visually look like they have a gap even though the string doesn't contain one. Unicode subscript digits were designed as standalone symbols (e.g. for chemical formulas), not for reliably chaining multi-digit numbers, so rendering quality varies a lot by font/terminal.

Fixes: try a different terminal font with better Unicode support; if the output is going to a GUI/web context, use real `<sub>` markup instead of Unicode subscript characters; or, if you need guaranteed tight layout, render the text yourself (e.g. with PIL) rather than relying on the console's glyph metrics.

`--psm 10` tells Tesseract to expect a **single character**, but your crops contain multi-character strings like "15/0", so it's discarding everything after the first glyph — switch to `--psm 7` (single text line) or `--psm 6`. Also your whitelist only allows digits, but your expected outputs contain `/`, so that character can never be recognized; add it. Finally, add real preprocessing (grayscale + threshold, invert if the overlay is light-on-dark, since Tesseract expects dark text on light background):

```python
gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
_, thresh = cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY_INV + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)
results = pytesseract.image_to_data(
    thresh, output_type=Output.DICT,
    config="--psm 7 -c tessedit_char_whitelist=0123456789/")
```

If the overlay is anti-aliased/low-contrast, upscaling further (300%+) and a light Gaussian blur before thresholding often helps small scoreboard-style digits.

In `df.query()`, plain quotes around `'Type 1'` make it a **string literal**, not a column reference — you're comparing the literal text "Type 1" to "Fire", which is always false, so nothing matches (and can raise depending on pandas version). To reference a column name that isn't a valid Python identifier (contains a space), wrap it in backticks instead of quotes:

```python
df.query("`Type 1` == 'Fire' and `Type 2` == 'Flying'")
```

Backticks tell the query parser "this is a column name"; single/double quotes are reserved for the string values being compared against. If the column names had no spaces you wouldn't need backticks at all, e.g. `df.query("Type1 == 'Fire'")`. This backtick-quoting for non-identifier column names is standard `df.query`/`eval` syntax.

Build a per-month lookup of `position -> supervisor_position`, then chase the chain until you reach a non-vacant supervisor (handles multi-level vacancies). A plain `if`/`else` on a whole Series fails because comparing a Series to a string with `if` raises `ValueError`; you need row-wise logic instead:

```python
def resolve(df):
    out = df.copy()
    for month, g in df.groupby('month'):
        pos2sup = dict(zip(g['PosnNbr'], g['SuperPosnNbr']))
        vacant = dict(zip(g['PosnNbr'], g['supervisor'] == 'vacant'))
        def climb(pos, seen=None):
            seen = seen or set()
            while vacant.get(pos) and pos not in seen:
                seen.add(pos)
                pos = pos2sup.get(pos, pos)
            return pos2sup.get(pos, pos)
        mask = df['month'] == month
        out.loc[mask, 'Non-Vacant-SuperPosnNbr'] = df.loc[mask, 'PosnNbr'].map(climb)
    return out
```

Use `.map`/`.apply` per row (grouped by month), not a bare `if` on a column, and loop the chain rather than a single lookup so a vacant supervisor's vacant boss also resolves correctly.

`request.files.get('pic')` returning `None` means Flask never received a proper `multipart/form-data` file field — the most likely culprit is `mode: "no-cors"` on the image-upload fetch. `no-cors` restricts what the browser will send/let you read (the response becomes opaque, so you can't even see errors), and is meant as a last resort for simple cross-origin GETs, not file uploads. Remove `mode: "no-cors"` and instead enable proper CORS on the Flask side (`flask-cors`).

Also don't set a `Content-Type` header yourself when the body is a `FormData` object — let the browser add it, since it must include the multipart boundary string; setting your own header (even to the "right" value) breaks parsing. Your JSON fetch correctly sets `Content-Type: application/json`; don't copy that pattern to the FormData fetch.

Finally, chain requests with `await`/returned promises instead of nested unreturned `.then()`s so failures surface instead of failing silently, which will make debugging the actual cause much easier.

`between_time()` filters by **time-of-day** (hour:minute:second) repeated across every date in the index, not by an absolute datetime range — and it requires a `DatetimeIndex`, which you don't have yet, hence both errors. For filtering between two absolute timestamps, convert the column and compare directly:

```python
df['receive_timestamp'] = pd.to_datetime(df['receive_timestamp'])
start = pd.Timestamp('2023-05-29 00:15:01.000138338')
end   = pd.Timestamp('2023-05-29 00:15:01.138503551')
filtered = df[df['receive_timestamp'].between(start, end)]
```

If you'd rather use `.loc` slicing, set the column as the index first and sort it:

```python
df = df.set_index('receive_timestamp').sort_index()
filtered = df.loc[start:end]
```

`.loc` with a sorted `DatetimeIndex` supports absolute-range slicing directly, unlike `between_time`, which is purpose-built only for recurring intraday time windows.

Your print showing the production DB name means Django's test runner never actually swapped connections — most likely the tests aren't running through pytest-django's managed test-DB flow at all. `django_db_setup` only customizes *how* the test DB is created; it still needs `pytest-django` to actually be driving the run (via `@pytest.mark.django_db` and its `django_db_blocker`), and mutating `settings.DATABASES["default"]` inside a fixture after a connection is already established often has no effect on that existing connection.

Checklist: (1) confirm `DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE` picked up by VS Code's test runner matches what you expect — a stale/incorrect module is the most common cause of this exact symptom; (2) run `pytest --create-db -v` from a plain terminal to rule out VS Code-specific config; (3) verify `pytest-django` is actually active (`pytest --fixtures | grep django_db`). This looks like a test-runner/settings-discovery misconfiguration rather than something fixable inside `settings.py` alone.

Your algorithm is already O(n) amortized, so 6.5s isn't an algorithmic problem — it's the `print(longest)` / `print(max_num)` calls inside the hot loop. Console I/O is orders of magnitude slower than the set operations around it; on any non-trivial input those prints dominate runtime. Delete them:

```python
class Solution:
    def lengthOfLongestSubstring(self, s):
        seen = set()
        l = max_num = 0
        for r in range(len(s)):
            while s[r] in seen:
                seen.remove(s[l]); l += 1
            seen.add(s[r])
            max_num = max(max_num, r - l + 1)
        return max_num
```

A real (minor) algorithmic speedup: use a `dict` mapping char to its last-seen index so you can jump `l` directly to `last_index + 1` instead of removing characters one at a time, turning the inner `while` into an O(1) update. But that's a constant-factor gain — the print statements are almost certainly your entire reported slowdown.

Python 3.13 ships a new interactive REPL (PyREPL, adapted from PyPy's) that replaces the old GNU readline/BSD editline-based one, so it no longer reads `~/.editrc`/`~/.inputrc` or honors system readline vim bindings — that's an intentional platform change, not a config bug on your end.

Two options: (1) fall back to the legacy readline-based REPL, which restores your old `~/.editrc` behavior:

```bash
PYTHON_BASIC_REPL=1 python3.13
```

(2) stay on the new REPL: it ships its own built-in emacs-style editing out of the box (Ctrl-A/E/K, etc. work with no configuration needed), but as of 3.13 it has no vim editing mode — that's tracked as a feature request upstream but isn't implemented. If you specifically need vim keybindings, `PYTHON_BASIC_REPL=1` is currently your only path back to them.

Cython compiles one `.pyx`/`.py` module into one `.pyd` by default — there's no built-in flag to merge many modules into a single extension. To get one `.pyd`, create an umbrella `.pyx` that textually pulls in the others at compile time:

```cython
# all_in_one.pyx
include "module_a.py"
include "module_b.py"
```

then build only `all_in_one.pyx`. Note `include` is a textual paste (like C's `#include`), so name collisions between modules and any relative-import assumptions must be resolved by hand — it isn't a drop-in for arbitrary multi-file codebases.

Also reconsider whether fewer `.pyd`s actually fixes the startup lag: on first launch after boot, Windows Defender/SmartScreen scanning many newly-touched DLLs, or cold disk reads, is a more common cause than raw file count. Excluding the app's install folder from real-time antivirus scanning, or warming the files into the OS cache, often helps more directly than consolidating extensions.

"Temporary object" isn't Python-specific jargon so much as general OOP terminology (borrowed from C++) for an object that exists only transiently to complete one expression, with nothing keeping a reference to it afterward, so it's garbage-collected almost immediately.

In the `super()` context: `super()` doesn't return your class or the parent class itself — it returns a lightweight **proxy object** bound to the current instance/class, whose job is to forward attribute/method lookups to the next class in the MRO. You typically don't assign it to a variable and reuse it; you call it once, e.g. `super().__init__()`, and as soon as that statement finishes, nothing references the proxy anymore and it's discarded.

That's the "temporary" part: unlike `self`, which persists for the object's whole lifetime, the object `super()` returns exists just long enough to make one delegated call and is then thrown away.

OpenCV's ArUco/ChArUco detector expects dark markers on a light background — its internal adaptive thresholding is tuned around that polarity — so a color-inverted board (light markers on a dark background) will generally fail or badly under-detect with default parameters.

Rather than fighting the detector's thresholding, just invert the captured frame back to the expected polarity before detection:

```python
inverted = cv2.bitwise_not(frame)
corners, ids, rejected = cv2.aruco.detectMarkers(inverted, dictionary, parameters=params)
```

If you must detect directly on the inverted image (no access to invert at capture time), you can instead tune `DetectorParameters`, particularly `adaptiveThreshWinSizeMin/Max/Step` and `adaptiveThreshConstant`, but this is fragile and generally less robust than simply inverting the frame first, which is the standard, reliable fix for this exact scenario.

Build coordinate grids with `np.mgrid`/`np.meshgrid`, then evaluate a Gaussian centered at `(3, 5)`:

```python
import numpy as np
rows, cols = 10, 10
y, x = np.mgrid[0:rows, 0:cols]
cy, cx = 3, 5          # peak location (row, col)
sigma = 1.5
gauss = np.exp(-(((x - cx) ** 2 + (y - cy) ** 2) / (2 * sigma ** 2)))
```

This gives a 10x10 array peaked at `(3, 5)` you can use directly as a feature. For a normalized bivariate density instead of an unnormalized bump:

```python
from scipy.stats import multivariate_normal
pos = np.dstack((x, y))
gauss = multivariate_normal(mean=[cx, cy], cov=[[sigma**2, 0], [0, sigma**2]]).pdf(pos)
```

Note `np.mgrid[0:rows, 0:cols]` returns `(row, col)` order — double check whether "(3, 5)" means row 3/col 5 or the reverse for your data, and swap `cy`/`cx` accordingly.

Ultralytics' trainer spawns DataLoader worker subprocesses, and on Windows any script that starts new processes must be guarded by `if __name__ == "__main__":` — otherwise each spawned child re-imports and re-executes your entire top-level script, including the `model.train(...)` call itself, which is exactly the bootstrapping error you're seeing. Fix:

```python
from ultralytics import YOLO
import multiprocessing

def main():
    model = YOLO("yolov8n.yaml")
    results = model.train(data="config.yaml", epochs=2)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    multiprocessing.freeze_support()
    main()
```

This is the standard Windows `multiprocessing` "spawn" requirement, not YOLO-specific — it's triggered here because Ultralytics uses multiple DataLoader workers by default. As a quick workaround you can also set `workers=0` in `model.train(...)` to avoid subprocesses entirely, but the `__main__` guard is the correct fix and lets you keep multi-worker loading.

No — LSTMs have no architectural requirement for a full single-sample sliding-window shift; the shift you use to build training windows is a data-generation choice, not a model constraint. What it actually controls is the **size and diversity of your training set**: a 1-sample shift produces many more, highly overlapping (redundant) windows than a full 1024-sample non-overlapping shift, trading dataset size/generation cost against phase-coverage.

The question that matters is whether your test-time inputs can start at arbitrary phase relative to your window boundary. If generated signals always begin at a consistent phase, non-overlapping full-window shifts are fine. If the same underlying parameters can produce the oscillation starting at different offsets within the window, small-stride augmentation helps the network generalize to that phase misalignment, since otherwise it only ever sees one alignment per signal.

In short: choose the shift based on how phase-sensitive your real test inputs are, not because dense shifting is required for correct parameter identification.
